newsitem.title: USA: Studies differ on breast cancer drug tamoxifen.
newsitem.headline: Studies differ on breast cancer drug tamoxifen.

text.p: The question of how many years breast cancer patients should take the drug tamoxifen got murkier with the release of the latest data Tuesday.

Doctors agree that tamoxifen reduces the risk of breast cancer's spread or recurrence. But there has been intense debate for years about how long women should take it, partly because of the slight risk of getting uterine cancer from the drug. Recommendations have ranged from two to 10 years.
There is growing evidence that two years is not enough but disagreement over whether five years is sufficient or whether therapy should continue for up to 10.
Zeneca Group Plc. is the main manufacturer of tamoxifen.
Just a month ago, two studies in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute strongly suggested that women with early breast cancer should take tamoxifen for five years.

This week the same journal is publishing two other studies suggesting that some women might benefit from 10 years on the drug. Those data are early reports from long-term studies that are still under way.

"To answer this question reliably, much larger trials than these are needed," said Richard Peto of the Imperial Cancer Research Fund in London and Oxford University, who wrote an editorial accompanying the reports in the journal.

"Every year almost one million women develop breast cancer, and premature certainties as to whether adjuvant tamoxifen therapy should be stopped after 5 years could lead to many unnecessary deaths," he wrote.

One of the studies by the British Cancer Research Campaign Breast Cancer Trials Group compared two years with five years. Its authors said more research was needed, but the optimal time could be as long as 10 years.
The second study was by the U.S. Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group. That preliminary data hinted that five years might not be enough.
